lead: Every row is a program you can read and rerun. The first five are recipes from the literature, ported here and tuned on the dev split. Everything after them came from a Claude Code agent, through the same gate.

html.agents-body:
{attempts} fresh Claude Code sessions ran one after another, each with Opus 5.5 at high effort, 40 minutes on a 4-core VM, and the current record to start from. The test split was zeroed in each agent's copy of the data, so a claim first met test data in the rerun, in a separate CI job, after the session had ended.

{records} of {claims} claims cleared the record rule, with gains falling from {best_gain} to {gain_last} bits per byte. All {survived} replicated on 8 fresh seeds (Wilson 95% interval {claim_lo} to {claim_hi}, and {attempt_survived} of {attempts} attempts, {attempt_lo} to {attempt_hi}), but that count could hardly have come out otherwise. Dev and test are a random split of one file, and in simulation, had every claim been exact, all {claims} would replicate with probability above 0.999, and at half the claimed gain still about {p_half}. So it mainly rules out a broken pipeline or misreported dev means, and says little about whether agent claims hold where failure is possible.

{claims_table}

Claimed gains did not visibly shrink: median verified over claimed {shrink}, {shrink_below} of {claims} below 1, range {shrink_lo} to {shrink_hi}. The plan set no threshold, and shrinkage cannot be resolved at this size. Opus was chosen for the series after its pilot passed and Sonnet's pilot claim did not.

Every score reads the same 1024 windows, so every plus-minus here covers seed noise on those windows only. As a check, each record from 05 on was rescored on the next 1024 test windows, which no score had read, on 8 new seeds. Gains from record {fresh_first} to the current one: {fresh_used_gain} on the usual windows and {fresh_fresh_gain} on the new ones. For the last record alone: {fresh_last_used} and {fresh_last_fresh}.

{fresh_table}

Each record also needs a written review from a fresh Claude session, which reads the code and logs and has to say what buys the gain. Much of the gain is tied to this track: about a third of record 07's gain (0.0061 of 0.0187, one seed, dev) sits in the first 16 of 512 positions of a window, and about three quarters of the gain in attempt-04's record 09 is eval-time modelling, paid for with 36.5% more eval ticks. A review can refuse a record, but none has: all six on agent records returned real, even the one that found the agent's account of its own change wrong. The briefs are in study/reviews.md.

As a check on the pipeline, each starting record went through it unchanged, 8 times over: {null_false} false positives in {null_n} runs across {null_records} records, which catches a broken pipeline and nothing finer. {null_refuted} run came back refuted, on record 08, whose stored batch of 8 seeds sits about 2.1 standard errors below the mean of its nulls, so gains measured against that record read about 0.0005 low. The sessions cost ${cost_lo} to ${cost_hi} each at list price. The plan, the count and the rule for each outcome were committed before the first counted attempt, and every session's transcript is in the repo.

The nearest precedent I know of is ARC's White-Box Estimation Challenge (2026), whose public leaderboard ranks estimators on FLOPs counted per operation by a metered NumPy wrapper, so an estimator reads the same count on a laptop and on the grader. It meters estimation and not training. Green AI (2019) proposed operation counts as a hardware-independent measure of work, and the MicroNet Challenge (2019) scored inference that way. I found no public record track that meters the training run itself, from about a dozen searches, which is not proof.
html.fair-body:
The reading is a function of the program, so for a program that does not branch on its floats, ticks have to match exactly. Scores pass through each machine's BLAS, so they can differ in the last digits. These are the same seeds of the current record on {fair_machines} machines, compared with the first, against a tolerance of {tolerance} bits per byte that was fixed before the machines ran.

{fair_table}

The largest difference is {fair_max} bits per byte, about {fair_ratio} times below the record margin of 0.002. {branch_note} In a browser the demo above reads the same tick as native code.
html.cheats-body:
The repo holds {attacks} entries written to cheat: reading held-out bytes, looking ahead, keeping state between calls, getting compute for free, shipping data in the source, and breaking the verifier. A test pins the exact way each one fails, and the attacks README names each hole the suite found, with its fix.

Four still work, and the tests pin those too. sum(range(n)) is one counted line, so only the wall limit stops it. Python big integers do vector arithmetic for almost no ticks. A line with 2000 additions counts once. A look-ahead bonus just under the twin tolerance passes, for under 1.5e-4 bits per byte, 13 times below the record margin. The first three are free compute, but training data is rationed to 20,000 Python reads, so free compute has little to learn from. That it removes any score gain is my inference, and I did not measure it.
html.open-body:
• Built with Claude Code under my direction, including the engine, the verifier, the recipes and the harness, and fresh Claude sessions wrote the reviews. No person has run this track, so nothing here compares agents with people.
  • It has no memory or disk cap. The PPM recipe peaks near 1.2 GB.
  • The test split is public. prepare.py downloads it, the permutation seed is in the code, and --against gives a test score as often as you like, so a record rests on published logs and a review and not on a seal. In the agent series the split was zeroed in each agent's copy. The obvious attack is a table of test text in the source: the 4096-byte literal cap allows 32,768 bits against 524,288 scored bytes, a ceiling of 0.0625 bits per byte, 31 times the margin. How much of that a real table gets is unmeasured, and it would sit in plain view of a review.
  • Prices are close to time, not equal to it. On x86, 331 of 335 calibration rows sit within 5x of the median. A copying reshape runs about 7x over its price, and embedding and squaring run 6x to 7x under theirs. Prices were frozen once records stood on them.
  • The score is one corpus and one budget. A smaller alphabet that helps here would cost dearly on anything else, and the sweep above shows the order can change at other budgets.
  • At a seed SD of 0.001 the record rule passes a true gain of 0.003 about {rule_003} of the time and 0.004 about {rule_004}, so a gain of 1.5 times the margin usually fails. The weaker replicated test passes one seed SD about {rep_power} of the time.
  • The series measures one model, one prompt and one allowance on this track. It says nothing about agents in general, and passing it does not show an agent understood why its change worked.
